feed.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Stale Tip Relay

entry.title: Combined summary - [BIP Proposal] Stale Tip Relay
entry.summary: The staletip proposal introduces a mechanism to improve the visibility of stale block rates within the Bitcoin network, thereby providing valuable insight into the health and performance of block propagation. By implementing an optional peer-to-peer messaging system, nodes that support this feature can share data about recently observed stale tips with their peers. This collaborative project, building upon AJ Towns’ foundational ideas and advanced by contributors such as pseudoramdom and w0xlt, includes a [Draft BIP](https://github.com/pseudoramdom/bips/blob/staletip-bip-draft/bip-staletip.md) and a [proof-of-concept implementation](https://github.com/w0xlt/bitcoin/tree/staletip-v4). Stale blocks, which arise when two valid blocks are discovered nearly simultaneously at the same height, currently go largely unobserved due to block relay technologies like compact block relay and FIBRE, which focus exclusively on propagating the dominant chain. This limitation makes it difficult to detect issues like network partitions or adversarial mining strategies that can manifest as elevated stale rates. Technical specifications for staletip include the use of BIP 434 feature messages to indicate node compatibility, message formats containing fork points, compressed headers, and status flags regarding block availability. To ensure efficiency and relevance, the protocol restricts communication to blocks within 1,000 heights of the current chain tip and limits header sequences to twenty entries. Nodes cache up to ten recent tips, balancing information sharing with network overhead. The intention is to enable more responsive handling of chain reorganizations and provide a reliable diagnostic tool for tracking events pivotal to network stability. Parallel to the staletip initiative, there is a concerted effort to document mainnet stale blocks through sustained monitoring of long-running nodes. Since these blocks cannot be reconstructed directly from the network after they are orphaned, this ongoing documentation—hosted at [this GitHub repository](https://github.com/bitcoin-data/stale-blocks)—serves as an important resource for research and transparency. However, concerns have been voiced regarding potential increases in Denial of Service (DoS) and fingerprinting risks, since expanding the surface for block data exchange could inadvertently expose vulnerabilities or complicate chain management, especially in environments with multiple competing branches such as signet and testnets. The current design primarily facilitates the relay of a single branch at a time, which may not suffice for comprehensive coverage in all scenarios. Discussion around security highlights that while DoS and fingerprinting vectors are theoretically augmented by the introduction of new message types, these risks do not fundamentally differ from existing attack surfaces. Constraints inherent in the proposal—such as limits on branch length, message recency, and retained-tip counts—mitigate the risk of abuse. Furthermore, participation in staletip relaying is optional, allowing nodes to disable it if the trade-off between observability and privacy is unacceptable. Each message describes a single linear branch, ensuring clarity even when handling parallel chains, with separate announcements for each fork. A phased or incremental approach to protocol changes has been advocated, wherein only stale headers are relayed initially instead of full block data. This strategy delivers significant benefits by making stale block occurrences visible without immediately disrupting the incentive structure underpinning miner behavior. Relaying headers alone suffices to increase transparency about stale blocks and enables miners who temporarily mine on an obsolete chain to adjust more swiftly. More comprehensive changes—such as relaying full stale blocks—should only be considered after evaluating the impact of header relays, given that transmitting full blocks introduces additional complexities related to pool attribution and transaction validation. The reference implementation supports three operational modes: disabling stale relay entirely, relaying only stale headers, or relaying full stale blocks. Default behavior currently favors none, but there is debate over whether header relay should become the standard. Relay mechanisms affect propagation speed rather than mining incentives, as rewards are strictly tied to the chain with the highest accumulated proof of work. Relaying stale blocks improves transparency, helps dispel suspicions of block withholding during reorganizations, and exposes attempts at double-spending or censorship. Empirical evidence from real-world reorganizations, such as the two-block reorg at height 941880, demonstrates that block download and validation occur rapidly, implying that optimizing ancestor block relay offers marginal advantages. Enhanced transparency through stale block relay would have clarified network dynamics, reducing confusion and suspicion in public discourse ([bnoc.xyz](https://bnoc.xyz/t/two-block-reorg-at-height-941880/97/32), [x.com](https://x.com/wk057/status/2036674054971703361), [Stacker News](https://stacker.news/items/1460047)). Detailed records, including timestamps and transactions, provide robust evidence against allegations of malicious withholding, underscoring the value of prompt stale block propagation.
